extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys and IP office practitioners preparing/processing patent filings involving biological material
extracted.subtask_short: deposit of biological material for patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal requirements for depositing biological material (microorganisms, cell cultures, etc.) under the Budapest Treaty or national law as part of a patent application, and the rules governing availability and furnishing of samples. Covers what must be deposited, timing, storage/duration rules, information to be supplied, requester undertakings, expert-only access, and related procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves biological material that is not publicly available or cannot be described in the application so as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention, the biological material must be deposited with a recognized/international depositary authority and the application must contain pertinent information on the deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical required particulars: name of international depositary authority; date of deposit; accession/deposit number; information on characteristics of the deposited material known to the applicant; proof/certificate of deposit. Jurisdictional examples: Austria and Belgium require deposit under the Budapest Treaty and that the place of deposit and file number be specified; Canada and Chile require deposit with an international depositary authority and that the certificate be included or provided before public inspection; China requires deposit with an authority designated by the Patent Administration Department. Some offices require a copy of the deposit document to be filed at time of filing (e.g., Bulgaria/Cuba practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of deposit (deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit must be made on or before a specified date (commonly the filing date or priority date) in order to be considered effective for the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most jurisdictions require deposit not later than the filing date of the application (e.g., Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Croatia, Czech Republic). Some statutes/practices treat the priority date as the relevant deadline (deposit before or on priority date). Certain jurisdictions permit submission of proof of deposit within a short grace period (China: deposit made before or on date of filing but receipt/viability proof may be submitted within four months; Belgium/Austria/others allow filing of deposit particulars within 16 months in specified circumstances). If the required particulars are not supplied within the permitted time, the deposit may be deemed not to have been made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information deadlines and permitted late filing of deposit particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on when the applicant may supply the particulars of the deposit (e.g., depositary name, accession number, date, viability proof) if not provided at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of permitted timings: within 16 months from filing or priority (Belgium, Austria); up to date of an early request for publication; within one month after Office notification that inspection rights exist (Austria). China permits submission of receipt and viability proof within four months of filing. Chile may accept proof on request of the Office. Failure to supply within the time limit may render the deposit ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage / viability guarantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how long the depositary authority must store the deposited biological material (viability guarantees / minimum storage periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some national provisions specify long-term storage requirements (China: store microorganism at least 30 years per implementing regulations and Budapest Treaty rule 9(1)); Belarus: deposit with any IDA guaranteeing viability for at least the term of the patent; Bulgaria practice: duration of storage may be unlimited. Many country entries state 'No provision' in their national law summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of availability of samples (who and when can request)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sample of deposited biological material becomes available to third parties and to whom (e.g., after publication, after grant, or earlier to specified persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common rules: samples become available from the date the application is made available to the public or from publication; after grant samples may be available to anyone (Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark). Before publication some offices allow access only to persons with a right of inspection or to nominated independent experts (Austria, Canada, Brunei, China). Specifics vary by jurisdiction: e.g., Canada allows the applicant to file a notice limiting furnishing to an independent expert until grant/withdrawal/refusal/abandonment; Belgium distinguishes availability before first publication (only to applicant/representatives), between publication and grant (to anyone or only an independent expert if applicant so requests), and after grant (to anyone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions and undertakings required from requesters
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions a requester must undertake before a sample is furnished (typical confidentiality and usage undertakings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical undertakings required: (a) not to make the biological material or any derivative available to third parties; (b) to use the material only for experimental purposes relating to the invention (i.e., not for commercial exploitation) until patent grant (or until specified events such as withdrawal/refusal/abandonment). Many national rules make these undertakings effective during the period before grant, and some extend for specified periods after refusal/withdrawal (e.g., Brunei, Belgium, Canada). Offices often require a formal undertaking form and may refuse certification without it (Canada, BN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's option to limit furnishing to an independent expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may notify the Office that samples are to be furnished only to an independent expert (i.e., restrict general access until grant or other events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics: applicant may file a notice before public inspection or before technical preparations for publication complete; Office publishes the restriction with the application (Brunei, Canada, Czech Republic, Belgium). Requests for samples in those cases must be made by a nominated independent expert; where nomination is required, the Office/Commissioner may nominate an expert on request or where agreement cannot be reached the applicant's notice may be deemed never filed (Canada). Expert must give undertakings and often sign a declaration; some offices require registration or Office approval of experts (Austria: expert may be acknowledged by President and registered; Belgium: independent expert designated by competent judge if no agreement). Forms and procedures differ (e.g., Brunei Patents Forms 55/56/57).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for requests and Office certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural steps and forms by which third parties request samples and how the Office handles certification under Budapest Treaty rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Canada publishes a form for requesting furnishing (Patent Office Record) and the Commissioner certifies a requester under Budapest Treaty Regulations, sending copy to applicant; where applicant filed a notice limiting access to an expert, the Commissioner nominates an independent expert on request and agreement of applicant is required (Canada). Brunei specifies particular Patents Forms for various requests (Form 55 for furnishing request, Form 56 to notify intention that a sample be available only to an expert, Form 57 for furnishing where expert restriction applies). Offices may set time limits for applicant objections to a nominated expert. Failure to comply with procedural rules can nullify the restriction or the request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/patentee may impose or waive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant/patentee can require conditions on furnishing (e.g., expert-only, undertakings) or may expressly renounce such obligations, which affects permitted use of samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many provisions explicitly allow the applicant or patentee to waive the usual restrictions (e.g., permit use for other than experimental purposes) or to require the sample be given only to an independent expert until grant (Austria, Belgium, Brunei). Offices publish notices of such limitations with the application and enforce undertakings taken by requesters or experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may be required to comply with conditions or give security before Office certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Before issuing certifications under Budapest Treaty Regulations or permitting furnishing, the Office/Commissioner may require the requester to comply with reasonable conditions or to give security for damages for breach of undertaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Australian Patents Regulations allow the Commissioner to require, before granting the certification referred to in Rule 11.3(a) of the Budapest Treaty Regulations, that a requesting party comply with conditions including giving security for damages for any breach of the undertaking. Similar safeguards may exist elsewhere implicitly via undertakings and expert declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement/new deposit where original deposit ceases or becomes non-viable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a deposit ceases to be available (e.g., interruption or non-viability), rules for making a new deposit and notifying the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belgium: new deposit permitted within three months from notification; copy of receipt and patent/application number must be communicated to the Office within four months; if interruption due to non-viability, new deposit must be made with the same recognized depositary; in other cases another recognized depositary may be used; new deposit must be accompanied by a statement certifying identity with the original deposit. Other jurisdictions have similar provisions for replacement deposits under Budapest Treaty–harmonized laws.
